after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: A fitted rule must work on observations it has not seen.
after.content: Train on observations with known outcomes. Check predictions on observations left out of fitting. The survey covers predicting a number, finding structure, and assigning a category.
after.takeaway: Training data → fitted rule → test observations; three task cards

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: For many predictors, shrinkage is a candidate to check on held-out data.
after.content: The earnings example reports test RMSE of 1.4093 for OLS and 0.7379 for LASSO. Explain shrinkage, the objective, and penalty tuning after showing the comparison.

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: A tree makes different predictions for different groups.
after.content: A regression tree partitions the observations into groups with different predictions. Its fitted tree and test error give the split and pruning rules a concrete purpose.
after.takeaway: Partition sketch → fitted tree → test comparison → optional mechanics

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: Combining fitted rules gives another prediction rule to test.
after.content: Boosting fits residuals; bagging averages resampled fits; random forests vary candidate predictors; ensembles combine fitted rules. Compare their predictions on the same task.

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: Now we look for structure without an outcome label.
after.content: Without an outcome label, the output changes: lower-dimensional representations, clusters, mixture components, or association rules.

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: Classification assigns a category rather than a number.
after.content: Support-vector classification separates labels with a boundary and a margin. This formulation does not directly supply probabilities.

after.label: Proposed stage
after.title: Choose the task, fit the rule, and check what the evidence supports.
after.content: Choose the task and its output. Check supervised predictions on held-out observations. A useful prediction rule does not by itself identify a causal effect.

before.title: General equilibrium · PDF p. 14
before.alt: Nash equilibria: the general interior solution is expressed using the inverse of I minus phi over theta times the transposed network matrix.

before.title: Power-series expansion · PDF p. 15
before.alt: The next slide defines Bonacich centrality and gives the inverse’s power-series representation; the following page interprets walks through the network.

after.title: Each player responds to the other.
lines: Each player’s direct incentive is \(1\).
Each adds \(\tfrac14\) of the other’s action to their own best response.
after.note: Source model with \(\theta=1\), \(\phi=\tfrac14\), \(\alpha_A=\alpha_B=1\), and zero shocks.
after.cue: Each starts with a direct incentive of one. Each also responds to one quarter of the other player’s action.
after.label: A TWO-PLAYER NETWORK GAME
after.alt: Two reciprocal links between A and B, each with coefficient one quarter. Each direct incentive equals one.

after.title: Each round contributes less.
after.note: \(x_A=1+\tfrac14x_B\), \(x_B=1+\tfrac14x_A\). Both actions equal \(\tfrac43\).
after.cue: These are terms of the equilibrium expansion: one, then a quarter, then a sixteenth. Their sum is four thirds; the bars are not a timeline.
after.label: A TWO-PLAYER NETWORK GAME
after.alt: Successive contributions: direct 1, first round 0.25, second 0.0625, third 0.015625. Cumulative responses approach 4/3.

after.title: The general formula adds the same rounds.
lines: \(k=0\): direct incentives and shocks
\(k=1\): one round of responses · \(k=2\): two rounds
\(\widetilde{\alpha}=\alpha/\theta\), \(\widetilde{\xi}=\xi/\theta\); \(G^{\prime}\) is the transposed network.
after.note: Interior solution. This expansion requires \(\rho((\phi/\theta)G^{\prime})<1\).
after.cue: The general formula sums the same rounds across every sequence of links, including repeated links. Its convergence condition still matters.
after.label: BACK TO THE SOURCE MODEL

diagnosis: The general inverse and its expansion arrive before a solved numerical example. A two-player calculation gives the audience something concrete to recognize in both expressions.
changes: Solve a small case with the mechanism intact.
Show the contribution of each round.
Carry the interpretation into the general notation.
preserved: The source’s linear best responses and interior-solution formula. The example sets \(\theta=1\), \(\phi=\tfrac14\), \(\alpha_A=\alpha_B=1\), and \(\xi_A=\xi_B=0\).
deferred: The general network, heterogeneous incentives, shocks, and boundary equilibria follow. The geometric-series interpretation requires the spectral-radius condition.
practice: Find the smallest example in which your main force still operates. Teach it, then say exactly what generalizes.
context: PDF pp. 12–13 introduce payoffs and best responses; pp. 14–16 develop the inverse and network interpretation. The revision inserts a solved two-player specialization before that general solution.
values: Source specialization: \(\theta=1\), \(\phi=\tfrac14\), \(\alpha_A=\alpha_B=1\), \(\xi_A=\xi_B=0\); reciprocal links with no self-links.
Best responses: \(x_A=\max\{1+x_B/4,0\}\) and \(x_B=\max\{1+x_A/4,0\}\). The positive solution is \(x_A=x_B=\tfrac43\).
Terms of the equilibrium expansion: \(1,\tfrac14,\tfrac1{16},\tfrac1{64},\ldots\); their sum is \(\tfrac43\).

title: Teach one path before the full system.
dek: Read the unknowns, blocks, and equilibrium targets before tracing twenty connections.

before.title: Two-asset HANK graph · PDF p. 72
before.alt: A two-asset heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model: seven computational blocks, three unknown paths, three equilibrium targets, and twenty labeled directed dependencies. Several long arrows cross the diagram.

after.title: Three unknown paths. Three conditions to satisfy.
after.label: ORIENT THE SOLVER
lines: Guess \(r,w,Y\); hold the exogenous paths \(Z,r^{*},G\) fixed.
The targets are residuals \(H_1,H_2,H_3\), each equal to zero at equilibrium.
after.note: The full source reduces 22 endogenous variables to three unknown paths.
after.cue: First read the graph as a machine: choose three paths, run its blocks, and check three equilibrium conditions.

after.title: Follow one chain from production to finance.
after.label: ONE PATH THROUGH THE GRAPH
lines: Production supplies marginal cost \(mc\); the price Phillips block supplies inflation \(\pi\).
Finance also takes \((p,d,r)\) from equity and \(i\) from monetary policy.
after.note: This panel follows selected dependencies; the complete graph returns in step 4.
after.cue: Follow just this path. Production gives marginal cost, the price Phillips curve gives inflation, and finance uses that inflation alongside equity and monetary-policy inputs.

after.title: See what the household block adds.
after.label: CONNECT INPUTS TO EQUILIBRIUM
lines: Households take returns \(r^a,r^b\) and fiscal inputs \(\tau,w,N\).
They supply asset demands \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) and the wage-setting statistic \(\mathcal U\).
after.note: Asset clearing also uses p. The wage condition also uses the direct fiscal inputs.
after.cue: Now connect households. Their asset demands enter market clearing; their wage-setting statistic enters the wage Phillips condition. The two direct feeds remain visible.

after.title: Now read the complete source graph.
after.alt: The same complete two-asset HANK graph shown before. Every original node, label, and arrow is retained.
after.cue: Return to the whole graph. We can now locate the unknowns, trace an important chain, and see where households connect to the equilibrium conditions.

diagnosis: The source moves from simpler models to a much richer two-asset graph. At this jump, the audience must decode seven blocks and twenty dependencies while also learning which paths are unknown and which conditions close the model.
changes: Identify the unknowns and equilibrium targets first.
Trace a short chain before following its branches.
Explain the household connections, then restore every original edge.
preserved: The complete source diagram returns unchanged in the final build: seven blocks, twenty labeled links, three unknown paths, and three equilibrium targets.
deferred: The first teaching panels show selected dependency groups. The full graph, including equity, monetary-policy, and direct fiscal connections, remains the destination.
practice: Choose one path through your most complicated diagram. Teach its inputs, intermediate objects, and destination before revealing the surrounding network.
context: NBER Summer Institute, July 2019. The authors already teach simpler directed graphs: a Krusell–Smith model on PDF p. 61 and a one-asset HANK model on p. 71. This revision adds a bridge into the two-asset graph on p. 72 (printed slide 24).

title: Attach each limitation to the result.
dek: A closing slide should say which inference each limitation qualifies.

before.title: Closing discussion · PDF p. 40
before.alt: Discussion caveats: spillovers to comparison countries; endogenous tax adoption and rate changes; interaction with the EU emissions-trading system; external validity.

after.title: Near-zero GDP-level estimates leave three questions.
after.label: RESULT & INTERPRETATION

items.title: Causal comparison
items.text: Could endogenous tax changes or spillovers to comparison countries bias this response?

items.title: Policy setting
items.text: These carbon taxes coexist with the EU emissions-trading system.

items.title: Transfer
items.text: Would a different tax design or another country produce the same response?

after.note: EU+ · $40 carbon-tax increase · restricted local projections · the 95% bands include zero.
after.cue: The cumulative GDP-level estimates are near zero, with uncertainty on both sides. Here are the three questions that limit how we interpret and generalize that result.

after.title: Keep the full estimate and uncertainty visible · PDF p. 25
after.alt: Original cumulative GDP-level impulse response for a $40 carbon-tax increase. EU+ sample, restricted local projections, parallel-path assumption, four lags, 0–6 years, 67% and 95% confidence bands. Both positive and negative effects remain within the bands.
after.cue: This is the exact response the closing slide qualifies: cumulative GDP level, not annual GDP growth. Keep both confidence bands and the specification visible.

diagnosis: The closing slide lists valid limitations after the results, but leaves listeners to connect broad terms such as endogeneity and external validity to the estimate. Pairing each concern with the inference it limits makes the closing argument easier to retain.
changes: Restate the result with its uncertainty.
Translate each caveat into a question about that result.
Keep the original response plot available with its full specification.
preserved: All four source concerns: spillovers, endogenous tax changes, interaction with emissions trading, and external validity. The original GDP-level plot and both confidence bands are retained.
deferred: Other outcomes and specifications remain in the original deck. A near-zero estimate does not establish that the true effect is exactly zero.
practice: Write “What this establishes” and “What it leaves open” in equally plain language. Check both with your advisor.
context: FRBSF seminar. Results occupy PDF pp. 21–38 and are summarized on p. 39; p. 40 is the closing caveat slide. This local repair links its concerns to the cumulative GDP-level response on p. 25.
